passage: Rafiq had just sat down in the school library when a burst of giggles came from the table behind him. He stiffened. Was it his haircut? His torn bag strap? He kept his eyes on his book and did not turn. Ms. Vinita, the librarian, glanced up from the desk. The giggling girls were bent over a phone screen, one of them holding up a cartoon. Rafiq still could not tell. He picked up his book, moved one table nearer to the desk, and decided he would watch for whether it happened again this week.

qa.q: Where was Rafiq sitting when the giggles started?
qa.a: In the school library, at a table in front of the girls.

qa.q: What was Rafiq worried about when he heard the giggles?
qa.a: He feared they were laughing at his haircut or his torn bag strap, though he had no proof, and the girls turned out to be looking at a cartoon on a phone.

qa.q: What could Rafiq do if the laughter did seem aimed at him again and again?
qa.a: He could tell Ms. Vinita or another trusted adult what he keeps noticing, instead of only guessing alone.

qa.q: How might Ms. Vinita see the situation?
qa.a: She sees girls sharing a joke on a phone and a boy who looks tense, so she may want to check quietly that he is all right. 🙂

grounding: A pupil hears tittering behind him, assumes it may be about him, but the cause stays ambiguous and reporting repeated targeting is hinted.

passage: Gurpreet was walking to the water cooler with her friend when she heard snickering from the back bench. Her steps slowed. She told me later that she felt every eye on her plaits. I was sitting two rows ahead, and I saw Nirmala's shoulders shaking as she read something inside her desk lid, a joke book passed from another class. Gurpreet's ears went red anyway. She drank fast and hurried back. I don't know what she thought, but she didn't look at that bench for the rest of the day, and I wondered whether anyone should tell her about the joke book.

qa.q: What was Nirmala reading inside her desk lid?
qa.a: A joke book passed from another class.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet probably feeling when she heard the snickering, and what else could explain her reaction?
qa.a: She probably felt self-conscious, since her ears went red and she hurried back, though she may also just have been thirsty and in a rush.

qa.q: What small step could help Gurpreet after this?
qa.a: She could quietly ask Nirmala or a friend what was funny, before deciding the laughter was about her.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel if she learned Gurpreet thought the snickers were about her?
qa.a: She would probably be surprised and a bit sorry, because she was only enjoying a joke book.

grounding: A pupil hears snickering that could be gossip or an unrelated joke, and the observer shows it was unrelated while her reaction stays visible.

passage: Monday: When Anirban walked into class, three girls by the window tittered behind their hands. His ears burned. He checked his shirt, his hair. At break he learned they'd been laughing at a cat video. Wednesday: Snickers came from the back row when he answered in English class, and again when he dropped his pencil. This time it was the same two boys, every time, eyes on him. Friday: He found a paper stuck to his bag: a drawing of him with huge ears. The two boys snorted as he pulled it off. Anirban took the drawing straight to Sangeeta Ma'am. She kept it, thanked him and spoke to both boys and their parents that afternoon.

qa.q: What had the three girls been laughing at on Monday?
qa.a: They had been laughing at a cat video.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when he found the drawing on Friday?
qa.a: He felt hurt and humiliated, and by then was sure the snickers were aimed at him, since the same boys kept targeting him.

qa.q: Why was taking the drawing to Sangeeta Ma'am the right step?
qa.a: The snickering had become repeated targeting with proof, so a trusted adult needed to know; she acted the same afternoon.

qa.q: How might the girls by the window have felt if Anirban had accused them on Monday?
qa.a: They would probably have felt confused and wrongly blamed, since their laughter had nothing to do with him.

grounding: Shows tittering that was an unrelated joke and snickering that was repeated targeting, and a child reporting the targeting to a trusted adult.

passage: Tejas, you think those boys are laughing at you. Sit, and let your Yusuf Nana tell you about my first night at the hostel in Aligarh. I was eleven. When the lights went out, I heard tittering from the beds across the room, and whispering, and more tittering. I lay stiff as a plank, sure they were laughing at my torn trunk and my village accent. By midnight I was ready to fight all of them. Instead, I sat up and said, “What's so funny?” A voice said, “Nothing. We're scared of the dark, so we're laughing instead of crying.” By morning, the four of us were friends. Still, Tejas, if it's the same boys every day, you tell your teacher.

qa.q: Where was the hostel?
qa.a: The hostel was in Aligarh.

qa.q: What was young Yusuf feeling as he lay stiff in bed?
qa.a: Young Yusuf felt hurt and angry, sure the boys were laughing at his torn trunk and village accent.

qa.q: What choice did young Yusuf make, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Yusuf sat up and asked what was funny instead of fighting, which showed the laughter was nerves, not mockery, and led to friendships.

qa.q: What was the first night like for the boys across the room?
qa.a: They were scared of the dark and laughing to keep from crying, not thinking about Yusuf at all.

grounding: Shows tittering that sounded like mockery but came from nerves, and the advice that repeated targeting should be reported.

passage: Jomon was halfway through his speech at the morning assembly when tittering started in the front rows. He faltered. Were they laughing at his accent? At the stain on his shirt? He couldn't stop and ask; four hundred students were watching, and the principal stood right behind him. His friend Gautam, by the stage steps, caught his eye and pointed up, quickly, twice. Jomon glanced back. A pigeon was strutting along the top of the banner, right above his head, bobbing in time with his words. Jomon grinned, took a breath and finished the speech. Afterwards Gautam said, “They were laughing at the pigeon, not at you.”

qa.q: What was strutting along the top of the banner?
qa.a: A pigeon was strutting along the top of the banner.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when the tittering started?
qa.a: He felt anxious and self-conscious, worried the students were laughing at his accent or his stained shirt.

qa.q: How did Gautam help Jomon keep going?
qa.a: Gautam quietly pointed up at the pigeon, showing Jomon the real cause of the laughter so he could finish calmly.

qa.q: What were the front rows actually laughing at?
qa.a: They were laughing at the pigeon bobbing above Jomon's head, not at him.

grounding: Shows a child hearing tittering during a speech and fearing mockery, when it was an unrelated joke, so assuming the worst is risky.

passage:
When Aadhya walked into the school canteen in Pune with her new short haircut, a titter rose from the corner table. Her neck went hot.

Arohi squeezed her arm. "Wait, look." The girls at the table were bent over a comic, pointing at a drawing of a cat in a helmet. Not her, then. Aadhya breathed out.

But on Wednesday, and again on Thursday, the same two boys snickered every time she passed their bench, and on Friday one muttered, "Here comes the boy-cut." That was no comic. Arohi walked with her to Mrs Deshpande's desk at lunch. Mrs Deshpande wrote down the days, thanked them and called both boys to the staff room that afternoon.

qa.q: What were the girls at the corner table laughing at?
qa.a: A drawing of a cat in a helmet in a comic.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when the titter rose as she walked in?
qa.a: Self-conscious and embarrassed about her new haircut, assuming the laughter was about her; her hot neck shows it.

qa.q: Why was telling Mrs Deshpande the right step on Friday?
qa.a: The snickering was now repeated, from the same boys, with a remark aimed at her, and repeated targeting needs a trusted adult's help.

qa.q: How did Arohi see the first titter differently from Aadhya?
qa.a: Arohi looked before assuming and saw the girls were laughing at a comic, so she helped Aadhya calm down.

grounding: It shows a child learning that tittering may be an unrelated joke, while repeated snickering aimed at her deserves reporting to a trusted adult.
